subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Gambler's Fallacy: Luck Doesn't Have Memory
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Gambler's Fallacy: Luck Doesn't Have Memory.

hook.text: A roulette wheel lands on red 10 times in a row. You bet on black because 'it's due.' The wheel doesn't remember.

buildup.text: The gambler's fallacy: believing that past random events affect future random events. They don't.

discovery.text: In 1913 at Monte Carlo, black hit 26 times straight. Gamblers lost millions betting on red, convinced it was overdue.

twist.text: The inverse exists too: the 'hot hand fallacy.' If a basketball player makes 5 shots, we expect a 6th.

climax.text: Each flip, spin, or roll is independent. Probability doesn't 'balance out' — that's a human invention.

punchline.text: The coin doesn't know what happened last time.

quiz.question: What is the gambler's fallacy?
options: Believing past random events affect future random events
Gambling more than you can afford

details.summary: The gambler's fallacy believes that past random events influence future ones. After seeing five heads in a row, people feel tails is 'due,' but a fair coin has no memory. Each flip is independent.
details.whyItMatters: The gambler's fallacy distorts decisions in gambling, investing, and any situation where people expect random sequences to 'balance out' when they do not.
takeaways: Random events are independent of previous outcomes
A coin has no memory of previous flips
The law of large numbers applies to aggregates, not individual events

faq.question: Is the gambler's fallacy the same as the hot hand fallacy?
faq.answer: They are opposites. The gambler's fallacy expects a reversal after a streak. The hot hand fallacy expects a streak to continue. Both misunderstand independence, but in opposite directions. Recent research suggests hot hands may exist in some sports.

faq.question: Why do people expect random sequences to alternate more than they actually do?
faq.answer: People have an intuitive model of randomness that expects balance in small samples. A sequence like HHHHH feels non-random even though it is exactly as likely as HTHTH. Our expectation of local balance creates the false feeling that chance corrects itself.
